idiom_name: pure-virtual interface + final implementation class, collaborators injected by const reference
implementation_notes: The classic DDD structure maps one-to-one onto C++: declare the operation on an abstract base class with no data members, implement it in a final class that stores only injected collaborators and mutates nothing, and pass the interface as a const reference so the compiler enforces the read-only contract. This replaces the documentation-level 'stateless' rule with a type-level one, and free functions in a namespace remain the lighter alternative when there is exactly one implementation; choose the interface form when the algorithm must be substituted at run time (test doubles, policy variants) or stored heterogeneously.
pitfalls: A cached result or lazily-initialised collaborator in the implementation class is the classic accident: the service is no longer safely shareable across threads.
Collaborators injected by reference must outlive the service; declare the service after its dependencies in the composition root, or it dangles.
A virtual destructor is needed as soon as the interface can be deleted through a base pointer - the abstract base here is only borrowed, so keep ownership out of the service.

variants.name: Free functions constrained by a C++20 concept (static polymorphism)
variants.idiom_name: template parameter constrained by a concept + free functions in a domain namespace
variants.implementation_notes: C++20 concepts express the service's dependency as a named requirement and take the collaborator as a template parameter: no vtable, no heap allocation, and a missing operation is reported at the call site. The abstract base class is replaced by a concept plus free functions (or a function template) in a domain namespace, and run-time policy selection is replaced by compile-time selection; keep the virtual-interface variant when the implementation must be chosen from configuration or stored in a heterogeneous collection.
pitfalls: Static dispatch is decided at compile time: swapping the implementation at run time (configuration, tests with different fakes) needs the virtual form or std::function.
Concept definitions drift from the real requirements - too loose a concept accepts types that fail deep inside the function body, losing the error message the concept was meant to improve.
